assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Active site
items.clue: The region of an enzyme to which the substrate binds and where catalysis occurs.

items.label: Hydrolysis
items.clue: A reaction in which a covalent bond within a molecule is broken by the addition of a water molecule.

items.label: Catalyst
items.clue: A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up or permanently altered.

items.label: Metabolism
items.clue: The complex network of interdependent and interacting chemical reactions occurring in a living organism.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly describes how an enzyme acts as a catalyst in a cell?

options.text: It increases the rate of a reaction that could occur without it, and is released unchanged.
It is converted into product along with the substrate, so the cell must keep making it.
It makes possible a reaction that could not take place at all in its absence in the cell.
It transfers energy to the substrate so that the reaction is driven forward faster.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes metabolism in a living organism?

options.text: The set of reactions that release energy from food molecules to keep the organism alive and active.
A series of reactions whose rate is set only by how much substrate the organism takes in from outside.
A network of interdependent enzyme-catalysed reactions, each controlled through its own enzyme.
A set of reactions catalysed by a few general-purpose enzymes that act on many substrates.

questions.stem: Which process is an example of anabolism?

options.text: The formation of glycogen from glucose monomers by condensation reactions
The oxidation of glucose in cell respiration to provide ATP for the cell
The digestion of starch in the gut into maltose and then glucose
The hydrolysis of ATP to ADP and phosphate, which releases energy

questions.explanation: Anabolism builds larger molecules from smaller ones; the formation of macromolecules such as glycogen from monomers by condensation is one of the guide's named examples, along with protein synthesis and photosynthesis.

questions.stem: According to the induced-fit model, what happens when a substrate binds to the active site of an enzyme?

options.text: The rigid active site admits only an exactly matching substrate.
The active site closes around a substrate that keeps its shape.
The enzyme seizes the substrate and holds it without any changes.
Both the enzyme and the substrate change shape as they bind.

questions.explanation: Students should recognize that both substrate and enzyme change shape when binding occurs. The closer fit strains bonds within the substrate, which is part of how catalysis is achieved.

questions.stem: Catalase in liver cells increases the rate at which hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen by a factor of many millions. What is the benefit to the cell of this increase in rate?

options.text: Hydrogen peroxide could not be broken down at all without an enzyme to make it possible.
Toxic hydrogen peroxide is removed fast enough at cell temperature to prevent damage.
Catalase supplies the energy that the breakdown of hydrogen peroxide needs.
The reaction releases energy that the cell captures as ATP, as in respiration.

questions.stem: A yeast cell synthesizes one amino acid through a pathway of several steps. Why does this pathway require several different enzymes rather than one?

options.text: One enzyme could catalyse every step if the substrates were supplied in the correct order.
Each step needs a different amount of energy, and each enzyme supplies a fixed amount of energy.
Enzymes are used up as they work, so several are needed to complete all the steps.
Each step has a different substrate, and an active site fits only one substrate.
